dashboard_interp_html:

Every Treasury maturity is still flagged: the 3-month bill at 4.25% (z +2.31), the 2-year at 4.80% (z +1.97), the 10-year at 5.24% (z +2.29), the 30-year at 5.60% (z +2.29) — all higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months. The curve itself (2s10s, the 10-year minus the 2-year) sits at 44bp, a bear flattener from Thursday (Unit 1): the front end, which tracks expected Fed policy, did the moving, not the long end. The 10-year first reached 5.24% on Sep 28 and has sat there on 9 of the last 10 sessions; the last time it routinely traded this high before that was June 2002 (Today in history, below). Because today is a bond-market holiday (Columbus Day), none of this refreshes until tomorrow's run.

Real yields and credit are frozen at Thursday's prints, one session behind. The 10-year TIPS real yield (what a bond pays after inflation) is 2.87% (dated 10-08, z +2.07), and the 10-year breakeven (the bond market's own inflation forecast) is 2.35% (dated 10-08, z +0.24, unflagged). HY OAS (the extra yield lenders demand for junk-rated debt) is 3.15% (dated 10-08, z +3.53, this system's largest standing flag), while IG OAS (the investment-grade equivalent) is calm at 0.82% (z +1.31). That split — junk wider, investment-grade flat — is the live backdrop for CL-0041's test (Claims, above): so far the junk print hasn't given back any of Thursday's widening, but it also hasn't been tested by a fresh session yet.

The dollar and funding costs are both still running hot, by two different yardsticks. DXY is 102.21 (z +2.04): the 72nd percentile since 1971, 81st over the last 30 years — strong lately and fairly strong against the full cycle too. SOFR, the overnight rate banks charge each other (dated 10-08, z +2.36), is 3.87%. Measured against its own 72-year proxy record (SOFR itself only starts in 2018, so this uses the fed funds rate, its long-run predecessor), that's the 44.9th percentile all-time but the 66.8th over the last 30 years — a 22-point gap, because the full record includes the double-digit Volcker- and 1970s-era rates that the last 30 years don't (§4F). Read together: unusual lately, roughly middling since the 1950s. ON RRP (money funds' overnight parking spot at the Fed) is calm at $0.30 billion (z −0.52). The Fed's balance sheet and the Treasury's TGA still carry last Wednesday's weekly reading.

Stocks, which do trade today, open where Friday left them: the S&P 500 at 7,811.54, 0.10% below its Oct 6 record, after rising 0.59% broadly (the equal-weight proxy RSP rose 0.55%, in line with cap-weight SPY's +0.60%). The chip fund SMH fell 0.65% Friday, a fifth straight session behind SPY — still unflagged, but a trend worth watching against Tier 3 below.

Why this matters: every rate a saver or a borrower cares about — T-bill yields, CD rates, the 10-year that anchors mortgages (7.40% this week) — is still sitting at a six-month high, and that won't change today because the bond market itself is shut. The one piece of the picture that still trades today is stocks, and they open 0.10% from a record.

The chart marks why the series goes dark after today's print and shows SOFR's own long-run context: 44.9th percentile against its 72-year fed-funds-proxy record, 66.8th over the last 30 years (§4F) — unusual lately, ordinary against the full record, the same shape as several other series this cycle.
history_html:
The level, unchanged since Friday. This run's peak was Oct. 5's 5.31%, the 10-year's highest since May 2002; Friday's 5.24% sits just below it, held since Sep 28 (9 of the last 10 sessions). High against the last 30 years (87th percentile), ordinary since 1962 (49th) — every 1970s/1980s reading was higher.

Before this run. 5.24% last showed up even briefly in June 2007 (3 sessions); it last held routinely through May 2002. Real yields agree: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.87%, dated 10-08) has held at or above its own level since Sep 28 and, before this run, last matched that level in Nov 2008, during the financial crisis — at or above today's on 99.6 of 100 days since TIPS began in 2003. Cleveland Fed's longer model (1982+): 80th percentile of the last 30 years, 54th since 1982.

Is it 2007 again? June 2007 is the closest match: the 10-year, real yields, the term premium, and the IG credit proxy line up then and now. Three differ — the policy rate (5.26% vs. SOFR's 3.87%), the mortgage rate (6.53% vs. 7.40%), and stocks, far closer to a record now.

Speed, not just level. This year's 106bp rise ties 1980 as the 8th-largest through this date in 64 years. From the 14 such rises since 1963, stocks were lower a year later in 5 of 14 (near the normal one-in-four rate), and a recession began within two years in 6 of 13 — small samples, not forecasts.

Why this matters (client-ready): “Rates are high for anyone who started investing after the mid-1990s, ordinary since 1962, lower than any day of the 1970s or 1980s. When rates rose this fast before, a recession followed within two years in 6 of 13 — close to the normal one-in-four odds.”
concept_title: Putting the dollar cycle together: a four-question checklist for any DXY move
concept_html: Segments 1 through 4 built this toolkit piece by piece: why a stronger dollar is itself a tightening event, not just a currency move (segment 1); why rate differentials pull capital toward the dollar in the first place — carry (segment 2); how that strength exports tightening abroad through dollar debt and dollar-priced commodities (segment 3); and how to read today's level against the dollar's own multi-decade cycle rather than just the past six months (segment 4). Put together, that's four questions for any DXY move. One: how big, and against which yardstick — the 120-day z-score for the last six months, or the all-time and 30-year percentiles for the full cycle (§4F)? Two: what's pulling it — a widening rate differential, or a safe-haven bid that has nothing to do with yield? Three: who feels it first — non-U.S. dollar borrowers paying more in local currency, commodity importers facing pricier dollar-denominated oil and copper, or U.S. multinationals translating foreign sales into fewer dollars? Four: does the rest of the data agree, or is the dollar moving alone? Today's own numbers run the checklist: DXY is unchanged from Friday at 102.21 (bond markets are shut for Columbus Day, but FX and stocks aren't) — still the 72nd percentile since 1971 and the 81st over the last 30 years. Strong by recent memory, firm but not extreme against the full cycle.
client_translation: The dollar's strength right now isn't new and isn't historically extreme, but it's still worth asking who it squeezes: foreign borrowers, commodity buyers, or the international funds in a portfolio.

story_html:
A search for weekend developments (Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10–11) turned up nothing from a named outlet that changes Friday's picture. The SpaceX-spectrum story that dominated Friday's movers hasn't moved either: the deal, SpaceX's roughly $8 billion purchase of nationwide 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management for Starlink Mobile, still needs Federal Communications Commission approval, and no outlet this system could find reported that approval over the weekend (searched Monday morning). That leaves Saturday's on-demand edition as the fuller account of Friday's close; this morning's job is Monday's own: what's ahead this week, and whether today's standing data still reads “tightening.”

Today in history, below, answers that question directly: not stress. A genuinely stressed credit market would show investment-grade spreads widening alongside junk, and this system's own IG OAS (dated 10-08) is calm and unflagged at 0.82%. What's flagged together instead is the whole Treasury curve, the dollar, and funding costs — a textbook “tightening” signature (Unit 3's credit tie-breaker), not a risk-off one. Stocks, which still trade today, confirm that read: 0.10% from a record, not selling off.

This is a bigger calendar week than today looks. Today itself is quiet by design — Columbus Day closes bond markets, and the only scheduled item is a low-impact Fed speech (Hammack, per this system's calendar cache). But September's CPI report lands Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 8:30am ET (confirmed in the calendar cache and corroborated by outside CPI-calendar trackers), and a cluster of big-bank earnings — JPMorgan, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo — are reported, per 24/7 Wall St.'s earnings calendar, to kick off Tuesday before the open, with Bank of America and Morgan Stanley following Wednesday. Fed Chair Warsh is also scheduled to speak Thursday (high impact, per the calendar cache). Per §4E, Wednesday's pre-CPI edition will lay out what to watch rather than call the number, and log a conditional claim the Thursday edition grades against the print.

One honest gap: this system's web search could not confirm any Sunday-evening futures level or a specific Monday-morning press lead for today's open (searched directly; nothing from a named outlet surfaced), so none is claimed. The brief instead opens on what the state file actually holds, above.

Why this matters to the current regime: a “tightening” tape (rates, dollar, and funding costs all elevated together) meets its real test Wednesday — a hot CPI print would confirm the bond market's own repricing; a cool one would raise the question of whether the curve has overshot. Wednesday's edition will frame that test as a conditional claim per §4E, not forecast the print.
client_lens_html:
“Why didn't anything move today?” Bond markets are closed for Columbus Day — a bank holiday most people don't notice because stocks stay open. Rates, credit spreads, and the dollar are all parked at Friday's levels and will stay there until tomorrow.

“What happened to my phone-company stocks?” Still developing, not resolved: SpaceX's spectrum purchase for Starlink Mobile still needs FCC approval, and nothing new surfaced over the weekend. That approval process typically takes months, which is itself a reason near-term risk to AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile may be more limited than Friday's headline reaction implied.

“What should I watch this week?” Three things: big-bank earnings Tuesday and Wednesday (a read on consumer and corporate health directly from the lenders), Wednesday's CPI print (the test for whether this year's rate rise is justified by inflation or has overshot it), and Fed Chair Warsh speaking Thursday. Rates are already high by recent memory (87th percentile of the last 30 years) but ordinary against six decades of history (Today in history, above) — this week's data will say which read the market leans toward next.
